title: Whose layer is it anyway? A commentary on: Prehaustoria of root hemiparasites Rhinanthus minor and Odontites vernus (Orobanchaceae) produce lignin-rich interfacial deposits closely resembling those of attached haustoria
content: Many symbiotic relationships involving plants require close physical contact between their surface and that of another organism. The establishment of these contact-dependent relationships often involves the secretion, by one or both partners, of substances that play a variety of roles in the interaction. One of the most common roles is to facilitate adhesion to the plant surface, as in the case of insect eggs or fungal spores deposited on a plant leaf or stem. In other cases, such as the formation of plant-associated biofilms, chemicals released by the host plant serve as attractants to certain beneficial bacteria, which will produce their own secretion to then form the biofilm matrix. Moreover, the presence of interfacial deposits and secretions might serve the purpose of species recognition for host-specific parasites and pathogens. In this context, identifying which substances are released by which of the partners can shed light on developmental, physiological and even evolutionary processes involved in species interactions. In the cross-kingdom associations mentioned above, the identification of interfacial substances is facilitated by marked differences regarding cellular metabolism and cell wall composition between the partners.
